column3: The immediately preceding verse gives the same women a choice oriented to God, His messenger, and the Hereafter, followed by a great reward.
Its multiplication and noble reward show a broader pattern of generous recompense, though the action is charitable lending rather than the focus's devotion and righteous work.
It joins repentance to righteous action and return to God, clarifying that constructive action accompanies sincere turning.
It closely pairs faith and righteous action, including for women, with a good life and recompense according to the best of what was done.
The immediate counterpart establishes the doubled consequence of manifest indecency for the same addressees, framing 33:31 as the positive doubled response.
It directly promises a good reward to believers who perform righteous deeds, but lacks the focus's devoted obedience and doubled provision.
It explicitly gives reward twice and joins it to patience, repelling evil with good, and spending from provision, strongly illuminating the focus's doubled reward.
It opens the same choice addressed to the Prophet's wives, contrasting worldly adornment with the orientation developed in 33:29-31.
Faith and righteous deeds receive an unfailing reward, reinforcing the enduring positive consequence but adding no doubled or provision motif.
Obedience to God and His messenger is linked to the repair of deeds and forgiveness in the same surah, giving a close obedience-and-action parallel.
Its command not to obey disbelievers and hypocrites supplies only a broad same-surah boundary around proper reliance on God.
The passing mockery does not materially clarify devotion, righteous action, recompense, or provision in the focus.
Disbelief in God and His messenger leads to a prepared blaze, a clear negative counterpart to the focus's prepared generous provision.
Its doubled punishment is a contrastive parallel to the doubled reward in the focus, though it lacks the focus's positive conduct.
Abraham is described as devoutly obedient to God, offering a concrete model for the focus's qanut devotion.
Prepared blazing punishment is only a distant negative counterpart to the provision prepared for the obedient woman.
Misplaced obedience to leaders leads people astray, offering a limited contrast to obedience to God and His messenger.
It broadens provision as God's assigned sustenance for every creature, but does not connect it to righteous action or doubled reward.
Its qualities for the Prophet's wives include devout obedience, faith, repentance, and worship, closely contextualizing the focus's qanut condition.
The account of people seeking to flee the battle does not materially add to the focus's positive conduct and recompense.
The reminder of a prior favor to Moses has no material link beyond the incidental repetition term.
It directly contrasts evil and righteous action, and promises believing men and women provision without account for righteous work.
Its doubled punishment for those who led others astray reinforces the same-surah pattern that elevated culpability brings multiplied consequence.
Mary is directly commanded to be devout to her Lord through worshipful acts, giving a focused parallel to qanut.
The twice-repeated corruption foretold for Israel provides a negative structural parallel to doubled consequences, but in a different setting.
The inheritance of land and property after battle does not clarify the focus's moral condition or recompense.
It closely combines faith, righteous deeds, forgiveness, and noble provision, making the focus's provision a consequence of the same constructive conduct.
The same surah promises believers a prepared noble reward at their meeting with God, closely echoing the focus's prepared generous provision.
The goodness given to Abraham and his later righteousness offer only a distant individual example.
Spending from provision is not sufficient to clarify the focus after the more direct doubled-reward and provision parallels.
Prepared humiliating punishment for disbelievers is a broad negative counterpart, already more directly supplied by nearer cards.
Marital compensation and household rulings do not materially illuminate the reward and provision promised in the focus.
The same surah shows disbelief making deeds void, a useful negative boundary for the focus's righteous action.
It combines faith, righteous action, entry into lasting gardens, and good provision, closely supporting the focus's conduct-to-provision sequence.
The command to worship God with sincere devotion sharpens the focus's qanut as exclusive religious obedience.
Its unfailing reward for faith and righteous deeds is a redundant general parallel after the closer reward formulas above.
The preparation of painful punishment after rejecting messengers is only a broad contrast to the focus's prepared provision.
God's sight of what people do in the same surah offers general accountability, without the focus's devotion or reward pattern.
Faith, the Last Day, and spending from God's provision give only a broad constructive counterpart.
Prepared punishment for denying the Hour does not add beyond the already covered negative consequence pattern.
It repeats the multiplied noble reward pattern for charitable giving, confirming abundance in recompense but remaining action-specific.
Universal qanut to God broadens the focus's devotion into an all-creation posture of obedience.
It directly joins faith and righteous deeds to forgiveness and noble provision, closely matching the focus's positive outcome.
The same women are commanded to establish prayer, give alms, and obey God and His messenger, concretizing the focus's devoted obedience.
The warning that association voids deeds supplies a strong negative boundary for why righteous action must remain devoted to God.
Faith and righteous deeds lead to garden provision, supporting the focus's provision as a positive result though without its doubled form.
Abraham's gratitude, selection, and guidance only indirectly illuminate devout obedience.
Provision and gratitude after rescue provide a general response-to-gift pattern, but not the focus's recompense structure.
Withholding God's bounty supplies a distant negative contrast to generous provision, without the focus's righteous action.
The correction of kinship and legal claims does not materially clarify the focus.
Faith and righteous action receive the best recompense and ease, a concise positive conduct-to-reward parallel.
Prepared hospitality and the description of Joseph as noble do not clarify the focus's divine reward or provision.
The prophet's refusal of human payment only loosely relates to the reward vocabulary and adds little to the focus.
It makes faith and righteous action part of a disciplined pattern of truth and patience, adding texture to the focus's righteous action.
Turning in allegiance to God, His messenger, and believers offers a close relational counterpart to devoted obedience to God and His messenger.
The battle narrative does not materially clarify the focus's condition or promised outcome.
The brothers' plan to commit wrong and become righteous later is a limited caution against separating conduct from moral standing.
Avoiding grave prohibitions brings forgiveness and a noble entrance, adding a related moral path to a generous outcome.
Full repayment of the true due on the Day of Judgment is only a broad recompense parallel.
Its disclosure and punishment of what disbelievers did gives a distant negative accountability counterpart.
Faith, the Last Day, and righteous action receive reward across communities, but this general formula is already well represented by closer cards.
Its familial and inheritance ordering does not materially clarify devotion, righteous action, or provision.
Universal devout obedience to God is a broad theological parallel without the focus's personal conduct and recompense.
It explicitly commands obedience to God and His messenger together with repairing relations, a concrete counterpart to the focus's obedience and righteous action.
The punishment of those who spread indecency supplies a useful contrast to the focus's positive same-pattern consequence.
Faith and righteous deeds lead to the gardens of Paradise, though this repeats the general positive outcome already established.
Repeated trials without repentance offer a negative counterpart to the focus's twice-given reward, but only at a structural level.
The battle scene and anxious suspicions do not materially develop the focus's conduct or recompense.
God responds to faith and righteous action and increases bounty, but the general formula is redundant after closer provision parallels.
The doubled punishment of hidden hypocrites supplies a meaningful negative counterpart to the focus's doubled reward.
Individual liability for the slander and special punishment for its chief show differentiated consequence, but not the focus's positive path.
The personal name Salih does not materially clarify righteous action in the focus.
Provision that is spent privately and publicly gives only a general stewardship counterpart.
Household etiquette does not materially illuminate the focus's devotion, righteous action, reward, or provision.
Repentance, faith, and righteous action leading to Paradise is a redundant general positive formula.
The request for a righteous child does not materially clarify the focus's righteous action or recompense.
The command to be among those who submit offers a broad obedience parallel without the focus's specific condition or outcome.
God's knowledge of striving and of what people do gives a limited accountability counterpart to faithful allegiance.
Provision for servants and revival of dead land supplies only a broad provision and resurrection backdrop.
The trust borne by humanity provides a broad same-surah responsibility backdrop, not a direct explanation of the focus.
The nullification and lack of weight for deeds after rejecting God's signs gives a clear negative boundary for rewarded righteous action.
Standing devoutly before God in prayer provides a concrete liturgical expression of qanut.
Faith and righteous deeds yielding joyful gardens is a redundant reward formula after the closer cards.
The command to use noble speech toward parents shares only the adjective noble with the focus's generous provision.
God's complete sight of what people do supplies a general accountability ground, without the focus's reward sequence.
The statement that none but God can remove the impending event does not materially clarify the focus.
Forgiveness, gardens, and the reward of workers give a general recompense parallel already covered by closer cards.
The queen's recognition of her wrong and submission to God provides a narrative conversion to devoted obedience.
The twice-numbered divorce procedure does not materially clarify the focus's doubled reward or provision.
God's provision from the earth and command against associates provide only a broad theological backdrop.
The hypocrites' denial of God's and His messenger's promise is a limited same-surah contrast to faithful obedience.
God as the best provider only generally supports the focus's generous provision.
Its ruling for women includes a manifest indecency exception, offering a nearby legal contrast to 33:30-31 but not their positive reward.
Provision descending from heaven as a sign gives only a broad source-of-provision parallel.
The river test and battle narrative do not materially clarify the focus after more direct obedience and provision candidates.
It distinguishes believers who do righteous deeds from corrupters, clarifying the moral contrast underlying the focus's favorable outcome.
Personal burden, purification, and return to God give only a broad accountability counterpart.
Return to God and being informed of what one did provide a strong accountability horizon, but not the focus's distinctive doubled reward.
Inheritance shares do not materially clarify the focus's devotion, righteous action, reward, or provision.
Faith and righteous deeds are recompensed from God's bounty, but this general formula is redundant after closer reward-and-provision parallels.
It explicitly includes devout men and women, righteous men and women, and a great prepared reward, making it a major missing parallel to the focus's female-addressed devotion and action.
The statement that the Prophet's wives are not like other women supplies the elevated-position setting that explains why their consequences are treated distinctly in 33:30-31.
The command to remember the verses and wisdom recited in the Prophet's homes closely contextualizes the women's obedient response in the surrounding passage.
The surah's conclusion distinguishes punishment for hypocritical men and women from mercy toward believing men and women, completing the passage's differentiated-consequence frame.
God promises not to let the work of any worker, male or female, be lost, strongly reinforcing the focus's gendered promise of recompense for righteous action.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds receive their rewards in full, a direct but general conduct-to-recompense parallel.
Believing men and women who do righteous deeds enter Paradise without injustice, closely paralleling the focus's gender-inclusive moral condition and favorable outcome.
Faith and righteous deeds are promised forgiveness and a great reward, directly supporting the focus's conduct-to-recompense sequence.
The Lord's good news of mercy, pleasure, and lasting gardens offers a close positive expansion of the generous provision prepared for the faithful.
Gardens of lasting residence are presented as the recompense of the righteous, extending the focus's provision into an enduring outcome.
Whoever seeks the Hereafter and strives for it as a believer has an appreciated striving, clarifying the purposeful action behind the focus's reward.
God does not waste the reward of those who do good work, reinforcing that righteous action receives preserved recompense.
A believer's righteous effort is not denied but recorded, a close accountability basis for the focus's promised reward.
Believers who are active in good deeds and hasten toward them add only a general action-oriented counterpart.
Faith and righteous deeds receive God's promise of establishment and secure worship, broadening the worldly consequence of obedient conduct.
Belief and righteous deeds bring expiation and recompense according to the best deeds, closely echoing the focus's favorable return for action.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds are lodged in lasting gardens, a direct but general positive outcome parallel.
Faith and righteous deeds lead to gardens of bliss, reinforcing the focus's promised reward after its stated conditions.
Believers who do righteous deeds receive gardens as a welcoming recompense for what they did.
Those who recite God's book, establish prayer, and spend are paid their rewards in full and increased from divine bounty, strongly illuminating recompense that exceeds bare equivalence.
The patient are given their reward without measure, offering a close abundance parallel to the focus's doubled reward.
Believers who do righteous deeds are in gardens with whatever they wish from their Lord, a strong provision-oriented parallel.
Faith in what was sent down and righteous deeds lead to the removal of evil and the setting right of one's condition, closely linking revelation, action, and consequence.
Believers who do righteous deeds are promised forgiveness and a great reward, with explicit allegiance to the messenger in the same verse.
Those who believe in God and His messengers receive their light and noble reward, directly pairing messenger-faith with generous recompense.
Faith in God and righteous action bring expiation and entry into gardens, a concise positive counterpart to the focus's promised outcome.
Trust in God is followed by provision from an unanticipated source, directly strengthening the focus's generous provision motif.
God magnifies the reward of the God-fearing, supplying a close abundance parallel to the focus's doubled reward.
The declaration that the recipient's reward is granted and effort appreciated directly affirms recognition of faithful labor.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds are identified as the best of creation, directly reinforcing the focus's positive moral condition.
Their recompense is lasting gardens with divine pleasure, a major missing explicit reward outcome for faith and righteous action.
